title: I Built a Team That Could Run Without Me. Then I Found Out Why.
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Summer Mulder tells the story of building what appeared to be a high-performing, self-sufficient team in her first company—only to discover when conditions turned hard that she had built them for good times, not for genuine problem-solving. The team excelled at running existing systems smoothly, but had never been asked to solve real problems because the business's early success meant there weren't any. When competition arrived, demand cooled, her partner retired, and the pandemic hit, the team that had run without her couldn't adapt—not because they lacked talent but because calm years had never required them to develop adaptive capacity. Mulder's central insight is that a team that executes smoothly in good conditions and a team that can handle anything look identical on a good day; you only find out which one you built when things get hard. Her prescription for leaders whose businesses are currently doing well: that is exactly when to hand people real problems, real decisions, and real consequences—at low stakes while you can still afford clumsy attempts—so the adaptive muscle is built before the hard season arrives.
points: A team that executes smoothly in good conditions and a team that could handle anything look identical on a good day—the difference only becomes visible when conditions turn hard.

Mulder's team was excellent at running the machine when the machine was working, but had never been trained to solve real problems; years without hard challenges meant the adaptive muscle was never built.

Order-taking and selling are two different skills—her sales team excelled at the former during a period of warm referral-driven demand, and was unprepared when the market required overcoming real objections.
The prescription: good times are exactly when to hand people real problems, real decisions, and real messes to sort through at low stakes, building adaptive capacity before a crisis demands it.
The point of a team that runs without you is not that they can hold things steady when it's smooth—anyone can do that—but that when it gets hard, they solve it without everything running back to you.
quotes: We also learned early when we could afford to hire, and we hired well. The people we brought on took real ownership of their roles, in all kinds of ways I didn't expect and couldn't have done better myself.
For a long time I told that story as proof we'd built something great. And we had. But I left out the part that actually explains it. The business was easy.

That's the trap, and it's a sneaky one. When things are easy, a team that just executes looks identical to a team that could handle anything. You genuinely cannot tell them apart on a good day. You only find out which one you built when it gets hard, and by then it's a rough time to be finding out.

Good is exactly when to hand people real problems. Not just tasks to run, but things to figure out, decisions to own, messes to sort through while the stakes are still low and you can afford for it to be a little clumsy.

The point of a team that runs without you was never that they can hold things steady when it's smooth. Anyone can do that. It's that when it gets hard, they solve it, and it doesn't all come running back to you.

I had a fabulous team. But I'd built them for good times and set ways. They were excellent at running the machine when the machine was already working. What they'd never been trained to do was solve a real problem, because for years we barely had any.
